name: Blow dryer + round brush
lead: A blow dryer (hair dryer) is an electric device that blows warm or hot air over hair, and a round brush is a cylindrical brush used to hold hair under tension and curve as it dries. Together they are used to dry hair and to shape it, adding lift at the roots and body that air-drying does not usually give. Wikipedia explains that dryers speed up and control the formation of temporary hydrogen bonds in each strand, which give hair its shape until moisture or washing breaks them [1].

The pairing is widely used for fine or thinning hair, where lift at the crown and hairline can make hair look fuller. Results last until the next wash or until humidity relaxes the style. Heat is the main documented concern: laboratory work on hair tresses has shown lifted and detached cuticles after simulated repeated blow-drying [3]. No clinical study of blow-drying with a round brush as a method of looking thicker or more attractive was identified.

paras: Most hair dryers contain a heating element and a fan. Wikipedia reports that many modern models use ceramic heating elements for rapid heat, include a cool-shot button that blows unheated air to help set a style, and offer ionic operation, though the benefit of ionic technology is debated [1]. Attachments include diffusers, concentrator nozzles and comb nozzles. A hot-air brush combines a dryer and a round brush in one tool, in rotating and static versions [1]. Round brushes come in different barrel diameters and bristle materials, chosen to suit hair length and the amount of curl or volume wanted.

According to Wikipedia, the French stylist Alexandre Godefroy invented the first hair dryer in 1888 as a seated bonnet connected to a gas stove chimney for use in his salon, and the Armenian American inventor Gabriel Kazanjian patented a dryer in the United States in 1911 [1]. Handheld household dryers appeared around 1920, initially heavy at about 1 kg, low-powered at about 100 W and prone to overheating and electric shock; the US Consumer Product Safety Commission has required ground fault circuit interrupters on dryers since 1991, and the number of reported dryer-related deaths fell afterwards [1]. Modern dryers can draw up to about 2,000 W [1].

Heat evaporates water from the hair and temporarily breaks hydrogen bonds in keratin. When the hair is cooled while held in a lifted or curved shape by the brush, the bonds re-form in that shape and hold until moisture returns [1]. The brush adds tension and root lift; the style resets with washing [1].
No studies found on blow-drying with a round brush as an appearance technique in people.

A 2025 laboratory study of virgin hair tresses simulated about one month of daily home drying by blow-drying wet tresses from 10 cm on the highest setting for 30 cycles. Electron microscopy showed lifted or detached cuticles with some fragmentation, and the contact angle fell from about 130 degrees to 92 degrees, compared with undamaged hair. The authors, who were developing a model for testing heat-repair products, tested only one hair type, and the corresponding author was affiliated with the company that sponsored the work [3].

The main hair-related concern reported in laboratory work is cuticle damage, which increases with heat [3]. A long-hair forum thread discusses a study comparing dryer use with air-drying [4]; the laboratory study above did not test protective techniques. Hair dryer burns have been described in case reports, including children's injuries from home dryers [2]. Electrical safety features such as ground fault circuit interrupters became mandatory in the US in 1991 [1].

Blow-drying for volume is frequently discussed in men's hair and thinning-hair routines as a styling technique rather than a treatment. Hair-care forums also debate heat damage and whether air-drying is gentler [4].

timeline.event: Alexandre Godefroy invents the first hair dryer, a seated salon hood [1].
Gabriel Kazanjian patents a hair dryer in the United States [1].
Handheld household hair dryers go on sale [1].
US requirement for ground fault circuit interrupters on hair dryers begins [1].
Laboratory study models cuticle damage from a simulated month of daily blow-drying [3].

lore.intro: Blow-drying is discussed as a basic technique for adding volume and as a source of heat damage, with threads debating dryer use versus air-drying [4].

claims.claim: Blow-drying with a round brush gives root lift and a fuller look
claims.believers: Styling guides and forum users present it as the standard way to add volume to fine or thinning hair.
claims.experts: The hydrogen-bond mechanism of temporary hair shaping is described in reference sources, but no human study has tested the effect on perceived thickness [1].

claims.believers: Forum discussion frequently raises heat damage and compares dryer use with air-drying [4].
claims.experts: A laboratory study found lifted and detached cuticles after simulated repeated drying of tresses, though it used one hair type and industry-affiliated authors [3].
